summary: Describes the Hostnames Server, a service that delivers machine-readable name and address information about networks, gateways and hosts. Replaced by RFC 953.

plainLanguage.summary: A helper computer you can ask for its list of names and addresses, like asking a receptionist for the directory.

questions: how to get host name table from server
subtitle: A simple text query service on the SRI-NIC machine that handed out the internet host name and address table.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the ARPANET and the growing internet needed machine-readable name and address information for networks, gateways and hosts.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to port 101 on SRI-NIC, sends one text query such as HNAME, HADDR or ALL, and reads back entries that follow the host table format of RFC 810.
tldr.outcome: The RFC calls central administration of one global host table with this server an interim solution on the way to a distributed name service. It was replaced by RFC 953.

today: RFC 811 has been obsoleted by RFC 953, so it no longer describes the current form of this service.

sections.title: The NIC Hostnames Server
sections.content: The Hostnames Server is a program and protocol running on the SRI-NIC machine, one of several name services kept by the Network Information Center at SRI International. It delivers name and address information about networks, gateways, hosts and eventually domains, as described in the DoD Internet Host Table Specification (RFC 810).
sections.plainLanguage: It is a lookup desk run by one office. You ask it a name and it tells you the address.

sections.title: Queries and Responses
sections.content:
A query is a line of text of the form <command key> <argument(s)> [<options>]. The command keys are HNAME (find an entry by name), HADDR (find an entry by address) and ALL (return the whole table). A response has the form <response key> : <rest of response>.

The response keys are ERR, NET, GATEWAY, HOST, BEGIN and END. An ALL request returns BEGIN:, the table, then END:. A response can span several lines, and continuation lines begin with at least one space.
sections.plainLanguage: You write a short question on a card. The answer comes back on a card that starts with a word saying what kind of answer it is.

sections.title: Using the Server
sections.content:
A program connects to the service host SRI-NIC at TCP port 101 decimal (or NCP socket 101 for the initial connection), sends the query and waits for the reply. Clients should take care to tell a single-record reply from a multiple-record one. HNAME or HADDR usually return one HOST record, or a BEGIN: list and END: if there is more than one match.

The RFC's example is HNAME SRI-NIC, answered by a HOST line giving address 10.0.0.73. An ALL request will likely return several hundred or more records.
sections.plainLanguage: You phone the office on its special extension, ask your question, and listen to the answer. If lots of people match, you get a list that starts with BEGIN and ends with END.

sections.title: Errors and Remarks
sections.content:
Any query can get an ERR reply of the form ERR : <code> : <string> :. The code is a descriptor of at most 8 characters that a program can use to react automatically, and the string is a message for logging.

The server runs over one global host name and address database, an extension of the old ARPANET Hosts.txt file. The authors see central administration with this simple server as an interim solution on the way to a decentralized, distributed name and address translation service.
sections.plainLanguage: If the office cannot find the name, it sends back a short code and a note saying why, so a program can decide what to do next.

items.label: Name not found
items.desc: The name is not in the table.

items.label: Address not found
items.desc: The address is not in the table.

items.label: Illegal command
items.desc: The command key was not recognized.
